title: Building a robot-learning lab from scratch at Bühler
paragraph: Bühler started around 165 years ago in Uzwil, and today billions of people rely on its machines every day for food and mobility. Yet it has no autonomous robots. After my semester project with them, Bühler trusted me with building a robot-learning lab from scratch. The strategy is simple: buy robot hardware and collect human demonstrations on real Bühler tasks, so performance scales with demonstrations, not engineering hours.

title: Kitting cell: VLAs on a real production task
when: Autumn 2026 · ETH semester project with Bühler
paragraph: For my ETH semester project I wanted to see what industry actually needs from robots, so I went into the Bühler factory and looked for problems robotics could solve. We picked kitting: bins of thin, translucent, poly-bagged packets (31 packets, 8 SKUs) that have to be organized into kit boxes. The goal is to empty these bins overnight, so the workers get them already organized in the morning. I built a bimanual YAM cell where a fine-tuned VLA (MolmoAct2, 183 minutes of demonstrations) grasps one packet out of the heap, then scripted code reads its label and places it in one of 5 bays. Around the VLA we built a loop that checks every grasp and retries every failure, so the cell keeps going until the bin is empty: in one long run it routed 25 of 32 attempts to a bay and sorted 100% of the bin in 49.7 min.

title: Sim-to-real RL: multi-cube sorting on SO-101
when: Spring 2026 · ETH Robot Learning (Prof. Oier Mees)
paragraph: In Oier Mees' Robot Learning course my team extended Squint, a fast visual SAC method, to a multi-cube sorting task on a real SO-101 arm, with an 80x144 wrist camera as the only sensor. Every policy was trained entirely in simulation and deployed directly to hardware. We trained a multi-cube splitting policy with domain randomization to separate tightly packed cubes, then chained split, pick and place policies with automatic cube-colour targeting. To bridge the sim-to-real gap we used FastSAM background masking at 75 Hz, closed-loop wrist-camera xy correction before each grasp, and IK-based smooth Cartesian descent. Ablations showed 100 Hz simulation beat 300 Hz. One lesson stuck: a drop-penalty variant converged to one-shot grasps in sim, yet about 80% of real attempts failed to grasp. We hit all three tasks on the real robot, including the bonus.

title: ETHRC robot-learning stack and the mimic-video pipeline
paragraph: At the ETH Robotics Club I work on the robot-learning team's bimanual YAMS stack. I raised the teleop control loop from about 30 Hz to 120 Hz with cProfile and multithreading, fixed a bug that read the 7 joints twice per observation, and tuned the leader-arm USB latency timer to 1 ms. I then designed POLARIS, the team's data foundation: validate YAMS episodes, convert them to a canonical format and build reproducible train/val/test splits, failing rather than inventing data. The team now trains on 863 curated demos across 9 datasets, and a fast data pipeline cut data loading from 110 ms to 9 ms per step. On top of this pipeline the team started fine-tuning Cosmos on our own YAMS bimanual data and is lining up the IDM training loop from mimic-video.

title: Towel folding and carton box: deployed ACT policies
paragraph: On the club's YAMS bimanual robot we run two ACT policies autonomously: towel folding, and putting a GPU ventilator into a carton box and closing it. ACT predicts k=100 future joint positions at once, a 2 s horizon at 50 Hz, with a CVAE encoder (latent_dim 32) and temporal ensembling over overlapping chunks. I trained it on bimanual data from 863 curated demos across 9 datasets, 347 towel and 516 carton-box. The hardest part was the lab's lighting, which swings from night with all overhead lights on to daytime sun with the lab lights off. I trained against an augmentation matrix of color jitter, gaussian noise, gaussian blur, random erasing and random affine, and sweeps across about 50 job configs showed which augs actually transferred to the deployed policy. We also disable autofocus on all cameras, because it adds non-deterministic visual noise to ACT datasets.

title: The ETHRC humanoid
paragraph: Next to my own bimanual work, I am part of the ETH Robotics Club while it builds its own humanoid, ETHRC humanoid revision 1, next to Unitree G1 models in the same description repo, and we recently started making him walk. The runtime, Argos, treats the robot as an appliance: a Robot API server with joint control, safety supervision and device services, where hardware and simulation share the same contracts. The hardware layer talks EtherCAT, Unitree and hand adapters, simulation runs in MuJoCo through humanoid-sim, and policies train in Isaac Lab on Newton's MJWarp or Kamino solver, with curricula, randomization and every policy evaluation kept in the learning repo.

title: Spaceship trajectories and highway merging
when: Autumn 2024 · ETH Planning & Decision Making for Autonomous Robots
paragraph: Planning & Decision Making for Autonomous Robots was my first ETH semester, and I finished with a 6.0. In the spaceship exercise our group planned trajectories with controllable thrust while dodging a planet and its satellites with a docking goal. We solved it with sequential convexification (SCvx) in CVXPY: each convex subproblem goes to ECOS, the trust region is updated by a factor of 3.2, the loop is capped at 50 iterations, and the nonlinear dynamics are discretised with zero-order and first-order hold. The final graded exercise was lane-change planning and control for an autonomous vehicle among human-driven traffic on real highway scenarios, sensed by a 360-degree 2D lidar. We built the stack by hand, with gap checks before a lane change, wall-of-cars detection, a PID steering controller and a PD controller tracking a 13 m/s reference speed.

title: Monocular visual odometry from scratch
when: Autumn 2024 · Vision Algorithms for Mobile Robotics (Prof. Davide Scaramuzza)
paragraph: In Davide Scaramuzza's Vision Algorithms for Mobile Robotics course, my group built a monocular visual odometry pipeline for the VAMR mini-project that runs on the Parking, Malaga, KITTI and Malaga roundabout datasets. Bootstrap initialisation detects Shi-Tomasi or Harris corners, tracks them with pyramidal KLT and estimates the essential matrix with RANSAC. In continuous operation the pipeline tracks landmarks with KLT, estimates each pose with PnP-RANSAC and triangulates new candidate landmarks once the bearing angle is large enough. My share was the 3D-3D correspondences problem, the visualization, debugging and the report, including a live dashboard that plots ground-truth poses and inliers and outliers. Parameters were tuned per dataset; on Parking the pipeline uses 500 Harris corners in continuous mode.
